meta.titre: The Glorious Revolution: why James II fell and what the settlement of 1689 achieved
meta.sous_theme: Causes, events and consequences of 1688 and 1689

sections.contenu_markdown: Whenever people speak of a parliament defending its rights against a ruler, or of limits on the powers of a president or king, they echo a quarrel that was settled in England in 1688 and 1689. In those years the English removed their king, James II, without a long civil war, and gave the crown to a Protestant prince on terms set by Parliament. Examiners ask why James lost his throne, what the revolution settled and what it left unsettled. This course gives the chain of events and the method for questions on cause and consequence.

items: In seventeenth-century England the king needed Parliament to grant taxes, and a conflict between Charles I and Parliament led to the civil war of the 1640s.
The Church of England was Protestant, and many English people feared Roman Catholicism and the power of Catholic France.
Divine right of kings was the belief that kings rule by God's authority and should not be resisted by their subjects.

sections.titre: The Glorious Revolution: causes, events and results
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Why James II was tolerated at first
James II became king in 1685 after the death of his brother Charles II. He was a Roman Catholic, but many people accepted him. He was no longer young, and his heirs were his Protestant daughters Mary and Anne, so the Catholic reign seemed likely to be short. Many Anglicans and Tories believed in obedience to the lawful king, and memories of civil war made people fear disorder. The failure of Monmouth's rebellion in 1685 showed how little support rebels had.

### Why he lost support
- He used the **suspending and dispensing powers** to allow Catholics to hold army and government posts despite the Test Acts, and he issued Declarations of Indulgence in 1687 and 1688 by royal authority and not by Act of Parliament.
- He quarrelled with the Church of England. In 1688 seven bishops who refused to order the reading of his second Declaration were tried and acquitted, to public rejoicing.
- He kept a standing army with Catholic officers and tried to obtain a Parliament that would support him.
- Louis XIV's persecution of French Protestants made English Protestants fear a Catholic alliance.
- In June 1688 the birth of a son promised a Catholic line of kings.

### The revolution
Leading men invited William of Orange, the Protestant ruler of the Dutch Republic and husband of Mary, to defend English liberties. William landed at Torbay in November 1688, James's support melted away and he fled to France. In 1689 a Convention Parliament offered the crown jointly to William and Mary after they accepted the Declaration of Rights, passed as the **Bill of Rights**.

### What the settlement achieved
| Aspiration | Result |
|---|---|
| Control of the crown | The king could not suspend or dispense with laws, levy taxes or keep a standing army in peacetime without Parliament. |
| Regular Parliaments | Free elections, freedom of speech in Parliament and frequent meetings were promised. |
| Protestant monarchy | Catholics were barred from the throne. The Act of Settlement of 1701 later fixed a Protestant succession. |
| Limited toleration | The Toleration Act of 1689 allowed most Protestant Dissenters to worship openly. |

### What it left unsettled
Catholics gained no toleration, and Dissenters were still shut out of public office by the Test Acts. The vote stayed limited by property, so Parliament represented the landed classes and not the mass of people. Ireland and Scotland were not settled peacefully: William defeated James II at the Boyne in 1690, and Catholic Ireland later suffered penal laws.

variantes.nom: Question on the cause of an event
variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked why people tolerated James II or why he fell, including multiple-choice stems.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Name the single most important cause or the one that best fits the stem, then support it with a second linked cause. For early tolerance use the Protestant heirs and the fear of civil war. For the fall use religion, the use of royal power without Parliament and the birth of a son.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When asked what the revolution achieved or why the Bill of Rights failed to satisfy everyone.
variantes.contenu_markdown: Group the results as political, religious and social, and for each say who gained and who did not. Close with a judgement: the revolution settled the question of royal power but left the questions of toleration and representation open.

sections.enonce_markdown: Explain why many English people who accepted James II in 1685 were willing to see him removed in 1688.

etapes.justification: Explain why with two dates asks for a change in attitude over time.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Plan: early acceptance, the actions that changed opinion, the final trigger, conclusion.

etapes.justification: The change only makes sense if the starting point is clear.
etapes.resultat_markdown: In 1685 James was no longer young and his heirs were Protestant, and many people feared a repeat of civil war.

etapes.action: Explain the actions that turned opinion.
etapes.justification: These are the causes that moved the political nation.
etapes.resultat_markdown: James used the dispensing power to place Catholics in office, issued Declarations of Indulgence without Parliament, quarrelled with the Church of England and tried the seven bishops, and built up an army with Catholic officers.

etapes.justification: A trigger shows why the crisis came in 1688 and not earlier.
etapes.resultat_markdown: The birth of a son in June 1688 meant a Catholic heir, so the hope of a Protestant succession was lost and leading men invited William.

etapes.justification: The conclusion states the link between causes.
etapes.resultat_markdown: People accepted James while they could expect his reign to end soon; when he threatened the law and the church and gained a Catholic heir, patience ended.

sections.conclusion_markdown: **Model answer (key points)**: In 1685 many English people accepted a Catholic king because he was not young, his heirs were Protestant and they feared civil war. Between 1685 and 1688 James used the dispensing power and the Declarations of Indulgence to favour Catholics, quarrelled with the Church of England and kept an army with Catholic officers. The birth of his son in June 1688 removed the hope of a Protestant successor, and leaders of the nation invited William of Orange. Tolerance ended when the king's actions and the prospect of a Catholic dynasty together threatened both the law and the Protestant church.

items.erreur_markdown: "The Glorious Revolution was a violent civil war fought across England."
items.pourquoi_faux: In England the change of ruler took place with very little fighting, which is why it is called bloodless. Fighting did take place in Ireland and Scotland.
items.correction_markdown: Write that James lost power in England without a major battle, but that conflict continued in Ireland and Scotland.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that William of Orange was a Catholic who conquered England.
items.pourquoi_faux: William was a Protestant, the husband of Mary, and he was invited by leading Englishmen.
items.correction_markdown: Describe him as a Protestant prince who was invited and who came with a Dutch army.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing that the Bill of Rights gave every person the vote and full religious freedom.
items.pourquoi_faux: The Bill of Rights limited the crown, but the vote stayed limited and Catholics were excluded.
items.correction_markdown: State who gained (Parliament and Protestants) and who did not.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing the Bill of Rights of 1689 with the Act of Settlement of 1701.
items.pourquoi_faux: The first limited the crown and settled the new reign. The second fixed the Protestant succession for the future.
items.correction_markdown: Give each its correct date and purpose.

items.erreur_markdown: Explaining the fall of James II only by his religion.
items.pourquoi_faux: His use of royal power without Parliament, the quarrel with the Church and the birth of a son also mattered.
items.correction_markdown: Link several causes and say how they combined.

items.enonce_markdown: State three limits on royal power contained in the Bill of Rights of 1689.
items.solution_markdown: Award a mark for each of three: **no suspending or dispensing with laws without Parliament**; no taxation without Parliament; no standing army in peacetime without Parliament; regular Parliaments and free elections; freedom of speech in Parliament.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain two groups of people who gained little from the settlement of 1689.
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for developed points: (1) Roman Catholics were excluded from the throne and gained no toleration; (2) Protestant Dissenters were allowed to worship but were still kept out of public office by the Test Acts; (3) people without property had no vote, since Parliament represented the landed classes. **Each group must be named and the reason for its limited gain explained.**

items.enonce_markdown: Assess the importance of the Glorious Revolution in the growth of parliamentary government in England.
items.solution_markdown: Plan: political importance (the crown depended on Parliament for taxes and an army, regular meetings, the Bill of Rights, the Act of Settlement); religious importance (a Protestant monarchy and limited toleration); limits (narrow vote, Catholics and Dissenters excluded, Ireland). Judgement: a decisive step towards limited monarchy, but not yet democracy. **Conclusion: it settled who held power in the state, not who shared in it.**

items_markdown: James II was tolerated at first because he was no longer young, his heirs were Protestant and people feared civil war.
He lost support through the dispensing power, the Declarations of Indulgence, the quarrel with the Church and the trial of the seven bishops, and the birth of a Catholic son in June 1688.
William of Orange was invited and landed at Torbay in November 1688. William and Mary became joint rulers in 1689.
The Bill of Rights (1689) limited the crown, and the Toleration Act gave limited freedom of worship to Protestant Dissenters.
The settlement left Catholics, Dissenters and the unpropertied with little gain, which is why it did not satisfy every aspiration.
